cards.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ, is writing to the church in Thessalonica along with Silvanus and Timothy (1 Thessalonians 1:1). He's looking back on the visit his team made there, and he reminds the Thessalonians they know it was not in vain. But before they ever got there, they'd already suffered and been treated shamefully in another city.

cards.question: Before Thessalonica, where were Paul and his team treated so shamefully?

cards.text: So they roll into Thessalonica, and there's strong opposition waiting. Me? After ONE burnt batch, I hid behind the cookie jar for a WEEK.

cards.question: After what happened in Philippi, Paul and his team kept the gospel quiet in Thessalonica to stay out of trouble.

cards.text: Paul says their appeal doesn't come from deceit, ulterior motives or trickery. Instead, they speak as people God approved and entrusted with the gospel.

cards.question: Paul and his team speak not to please men, but to please ___.
Paul says God only listens to their words and never looks at their hearts.

cards.text: So Paul's not fishing for a thumbs-up from the crowd. Unlike me after every batch: "You like it? You LIKE it? Be honest. No, DON'T be honest." Now Paul gets specific about the words his team used, and he calls God as his witness.

cards.question: Paul admits his team used a little flattery to win the Thessalonians over.

cards.text: Flattery is telling your boss his two-hour meeting just FLEW by. Paul says they never did it, and they never used any pretext for greed either.

cards.question: As apostles of Christ, Paul says his team had the authority to demand something they never went looking for. What was it?

cards.text: On the contrary, Paul says, they were gentle among the Thessalonians. And he picks a picture to show just how gentle.

cards.question: What picture does Paul use for how gentle his team was with the Thessalonians?

answers.text: A nursing mother caring for her children
A shepherd carrying a lost lamb home
A gardener tending his young plants

cards.question: Paul says his team cared so deeply that they were delighted to share the gospel of God and their own ___ as well.

cards.text: Then Paul tells them, "That is how beloved you have become to us." Friend, that's not some guy passing through town to give a speech.
Paul reminds the Thessalonians of something they saw up close: his team's labor and toil while they were there.

cards.question: Paul and his team worked night and day while they proclaimed the gospel in Thessalonica. Why?

answers.text: So they wouldn't be a burden to anyone
To raise money for the church in Jerusalem
To buy a place for the church to meet

cards.text: Night AND day, plus preaching, and here I am needing a nap when my oven timer goes off twice. Then Paul calls the Thessalonians and God as witnesses of how his team lived among the believers.

cards.question: Paul says his team's conduct among the believers was holy, righteous and blameless.

cards.text: Earlier, Paul compared his team to a nursing mother. Now he reaches for a second picture.

cards.question: Paul says they treated each of the Thessalonians as a ___ treats his own children.
Like a father, Paul's team encouraged and comforted the Thessalonians. What did they urge them to do?

answers.text: Walk in a manner worthy of God
Hold fast to the customs of their fathers
Separate themselves from their own people

cards.text: And Paul says it's God who calls them into His own kingdom and glory. Then Paul says his team keeps thanking God because of how the Thessalonians received the message they heard.

cards.question: The Thessalonians accepted the message not as the word of ___ but as the word of ___.
Paul says the word of God stopped working in the Thessalonians once his team was gone.

cards.text: That word does NOT clock out at five, friend. Then Paul says the Thessalonians became imitators of the churches of God in Judea.

cards.question: How did the Thessalonians end up like the churches of God in Judea?

answers.text: They suffered from their own countrymen
They met in the same synagogue

cards.text: Paul says those churches suffered the same things from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and their own prophets.
They drove Paul's team out as well. Paul says they are displeasing to God and hostile to all men.

cards.question: Paul says the ones who drove his team out were hindering them from doing something. What?

answers.text: Telling the Gentiles how they may be saved

cards.text: As a result, Paul says, they keep heaping up their sins to full capacity, and the utmost wrath has come upon them. Heavy words to close on, friend, and Paul doesn't soften them.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 8 quotes "You like it? You LIKE it? Be honest. No, DON'T be honest.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The joke 'Me? After ONE burnt batch, I hid behind the cookie jar for a WEEK.' sets Papa Dorin up as the opposite of Paul's team right after the opposition is mentioned. That tells the baker the team did not hide or go quiet, which gives away the answer to the true-or-false question on card 4 about keeping the gospel quiet in Thessalonica.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The card says 'Earlier, Paul compared his team to a nursing mother,' which tells 1 Thessalonians 2:7. It cites only 1 Thessalonians 2:11, and it tells nothing from 2:11 itself, because that verse's picture is held back for card 6.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Cards 13 and 14 retell 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16 faithfully: the Judean churches suffered 'from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and their own prophets.' The cards then say these people are displeasing to God and hostile to all men. The retelling follows the text, but a baker could read it as a statement about all Jewish people. The hard rule against putting down any group is written about jokes, and the Scripture rules say to leave open what the text leaves open and add no reasons. So the docs don't say whether Papa Dorin may add a short line of context, such as noting that Paul and the Judean believers were Jewish themselves or that the text means the specific opponents it describes.
findings.question: For passages like 1 Thessalonians 2:14-16 that speak harshly about a named group, should Papa Dorin add a brief neutral line of context (for example, that Paul himself was Jewish and is describing specific opponents in Judea), or should he retell the text exactly as written with nothing added?
